Braess's Paradox · Simulatio Lab
Run Braess's paradox yourself: simulate drivers choosing their own routes and see why opening a shortcut can raise everyone's average commute.
A New Road Made Everyone Slower: Braess's Paradox

It is easy to think that if roads are jammed, you should build a new one: more roads should shorten everyone's commute. In this simple road network, though, opening a shortcut in front of 4,000 drivers sends them all onto it, and the average commute grows from 65 to 80 minutes. Close one road and things get faster. Nobody did anything wrong: everyone just picked the route that was fastest for them.

There are two routes from start to destination: Route A (start→A→destination) and Route B (start→B→destination). Start→A and B→destination are congestible roads: the time grows by the sensitivity for every 1,000 drivers on them (10 minutes by default, so x drivers take x/100 minutes). A→destination and start→B always take 45 minutes, however many cars use them.
Opening the shortcut adds a third route (start→A→B→destination) that crosses from A to B. Crossing takes a fixed time (0 minutes by default) and never gets congested.

Each round, 8% of drivers reconsider their route. They switch only if the time they would get after switching is clearly shorter, and they move one at a time, so the system ends where nobody can gain by switching alone.

The lowest average time reachable if a planner could assign routes in the same network is the social optimum. The selfish equilibrium's average time divided by the social optimum is the price of anarchy.

① Watching the Commute

A road's thickness shows how many drivers use it, and its color the time it takes (green fast, red slow). When the shortcut opens, drivers move one by one to whatever is faster, and the bar below shows the share choosing each route.

The blue line is the average commute in each round. The green dashed line is the equilibrium without the shortcut, the red one the equilibrium with it (theory), and gray is the social optimum a planner could reach. The vertical dashed line marks when the road changed.

⑤ If the Shortcut Gets Costlier
The horizontal axis is the time needed to cross the shortcut, the vertical axis the average commute at equilibrium. Past a certain cost nobody uses the shortcut and it is as good as closed.

What it shows: With 4,000 drivers, a 0-minute shortcut and sensitivity 10 (x/100 minutes), the equilibrium without the shortcut split drivers evenly between Routes A and B for an average of 65.0 minutes. Once the shortcut opened, drivers drifted to it, the average reached 79.5 minutes by round 100, and by round 180 everyone (100%) used the shortcut route for an average of 80.0 minutes. At that end state, switching alone gained 0 minutes. Going the other way, closing the shortcut brought the average from 79.7 minutes just before the closure down to 65.0 minutes within 5 rounds. If everyone agreed to skip the shortcut it would be 65.0 minutes, and a planner assigning routes optimally (about 13% on the shortcut) reached 64.7, so the price of anarchy was 1.24. The effect depended on the number of drivers. Below 3,000 drivers the shortcut helped (2,000 drivers: 55.0 → 40.0 minutes), at 3,000 it was a tie at 60.0 minutes, between 3,000 and 9,000 it hurt, most at 4,500 drivers with 67.5 → 90.0 minutes (1.33 times), and from 9,000 drivers on nobody used it so nothing changed. With a shortcut cost of 25 minutes or more the result was 65.0 minutes, the same as closed, and at 5 minutes it was 85.0 minutes, worse than at 0 minutes (80.0). With congestion sensitivity 5 the shortcut helped (55.0 → 40.0 minutes), and with 20 it hurt (85.0 → 90.0 minutes).
